strengths: The paper identifies and clearly articulates a real limitation of spectral-feature NPIV methods (outcome-agnostic feature learning leading to spectral misalignment), building coherently on Meunier et al.'s 'good/bad scenario' analysis.

The core idea is elegant and well-executed: the augmented loss (Eq. 4/5) is shown via Proposition 1 to be exactly equivalent to learning the truncated SVD of an augmented operator T_δ, giving a principled interpretation of what is otherwise a simple regularizer; the proof (Appendix B.1) is clean.

The theoretical treatment is substantially more complete than typical for such methods: a high-probability 2SLS generalization bound (Theorem 1) that improves on prior in-expectation results, and a perturbation-theoretic approximation error analysis (Theorem 4, Props 5-8, based on Wedin's sin-Θ theorem) that yields concrete corollaries for both the 'good' and 'bad' scenarios, including a quantitative benefit in the misaligned regime.

Experiments are well-designed and support the claims: a synthetic setting with controlled spectral alignment, a thoughtfully constructed harder dSprites benchmark (h_new) with a careful empirical spectral-alignment analysis in Appendix D that justifies why the new benchmark is misaligned, and an OPE application demonstrating broader applicability.

The paper is honest about limitations: the optimality gap for DNN training is left open, the consistency of stage-2-loss-based model selection is explicitly argued to lack theoretical justification (D.8), and the rank-K extension is presented as preliminary. This candor is commendable.
weaknesses: The theory does not fully cover the practical method: the central bound (Theorem 4) is conditioned on the optimality gap ε_d(θ̂_m, ω̂_m, δ), which for neural-network feature learning is left as an open problem. Thus the 'comprehensive theoretical analysis' claim is overstated; the guarantees hold only for features that approximately achieve the population-level optimum.

The choice of δ, arguably the key practical knob, remains heuristic. The paper offers two procedures (loss balancing, projection-length estimation, stage-2 loss) but admits none has theoretical backing, and the projection estimator already degrades for δ=1.0 while performance is still acceptable — leaving selection partly unresolved.

Assumptions needed for the main results are strong and hard to verify in practice: positivity of the ill-posedness measure (Assumption 3), positivity of the gap γ_d(δ) (Eq. 8), and signal-to-noise conditions (∥s_1∥ ≫ λ_k^{-2}∥q_1∥) that essentially require knowledge of the alignment structure the method is meant to discover automatically.

Empirical comparisons are somewhat narrow: no comparison against minimax/GMM-based NPIV methods, which are natural competitors in the misaligned regimes where spectral methods struggle. In the OPE experiments, results are mixed (AugSpecIV performs well on Cartpole but poorly on Mountain Car, where DFIV excels), so claims of 'robustness and competitiveness' are only partially supported.

The methodological contribution — adding an outcome-predictive regularization term to an existing contrastive loss — is relatively incremental; the value derives largely from the analysis and the augmented-operator interpretation rather than from a substantially new algorithmic idea.

While theorems are stated with constants and proofs appear largely correct on inspection, some steps are terse (e.g., Eq. (8)'s derivation of the gap condition, and the second inequality of Proposition 7), and a referee may wish to verify the perturbation arguments more carefully; the writing occasionally makes the main results harder to extract than necessary.

strengths: The paper targets a genuine and well-identified limitation of spectral feature learning for NPIV (outcome-agnostic features, following Meunier et al. [27]), and the core idea is clean: augmenting the contrastive loss is shown rigorously (Proposition 1, proof in B.1) to be equivalent to learning a truncated SVD of an augmented operator T_δ.

The theoretical treatment is careful and largely self-contained: the perturbation analysis (Wedin sin-Θ, Weyl, Eckart-Young) used to relate singular subspaces of T_δ to those of T (Propositions 4-8, Theorem 4) is a real technical contribution, and the 'good'/'bad' scenario corollaries give concrete insight into when one feature can replace k spurious ones.
Theorem 1 provides a non-asymptotic, high-probability 2SLS bound that improves on prior in-expectation guarantees, with assumptions that are standard for this literature.

Experiments are reasonably well designed: a controlled synthetic setting where misalignment can be tuned, a new and better-motivated 'hard' dSprites structural function (h_new) whose spectral misalignment is empirically verified (Fig. 5), and an OPE application with complete protocol details (hyperparameter grids, seeds, architectures in Tables 1-5), which supports reproducibility.

The discussion of limitations is unusually honest: the authors explicitly acknowledge that the optimality gap E_d is not bounded, that δ selection via the stage-2 loss lacks consistency guarantees (Section D.8 even argues 2SLS-loss model selection is generally unprincipled), and that higher-rank perturbations are unresolved.
weaknesses: The end-to-end theory is incomplete: the final error bounds all depend on the optimality gap E_d(θ, ω, δ), which the authors concede is unbounded ('an open problem in its own right'). Consequently, Theorem 4 and the 'bad scenario' result do not provide a fully supported statistical guarantee for the method as implemented — the central claim of a 'full generalization error bound' (Contribution 2) overstates what is proven.

The key hyperparameter δ lacks theoretical or reliable automatic selection. The recommended procedure is an ad hoc heuristic (Section 6.4), performance is explicitly 'contingent on the choice of δ', and the alternative (stage-2 loss tuning) is, by the authors' own admission in D.8, unprincipled. This significantly weakens practical usability of the method.

The empirical case in the hardest setting is not decisive: on OPE, AugSpecIV performs well on Cartpole but poorly on Mountain Car, and the paper concedes 'no OPE method performed uniformly well'; the dSprites results for δ up to 1.0 actually show degradation relative to δ=0.3-0.5, and boxplots are based on only 9 fitted models.

The 'bad scenario' bound (Eq. 18) has awkward prefactors (e.g., a term scaling with 5∥h0∥/λ_k²·(∥s1∥/∥s1∥) that is not informative as written) and requires a strong signal-to-noise condition ∥s1∥ ≫ λ_k^{-2}∥q1∥, so its practical reach is limited.

Novelty is moderate: the method is a one-parameter regularization added to the existing SpecIV contrastive loss, and the perturbation machinery (Wedin, Weyl) is standard; the contribution is best viewed as an increment on Meunier et al. [27] rather than a new framework.

Notation in Section 4 and Appendix B is dense and occasionally inconsistent (e.g., overloading of bars/underbars in the partition decomposition, 'call' vs 'called' in Theorem 5), which impedes verification of the proofs; some steps in Propositions 6-7 would benefit from more careful justification.

strengths: The paper identifies a genuine and well-articulated limitation of outcome-agnostic spectral feature learning (SpecIV) for NPIV, building directly and transparently on Meunier et al. [27]. The 'spectral misalignment' framing is convincing and well-motivated.

The core methodological idea is elegant: augmenting the operator T with an outcome-aligned column (Tδ), showing the resulting contrastive loss corresponds to a truncated SVD of Tδ (Proposition 1), and reparametrizing with an auxiliary variable ω to avoid backpropagating through a matrix inverse. The derivation is clean and verifiable.

The theoretical analysis is substantive: a high-probability 2SLS bound (Theorem 1), a careful perturbation-based analysis relating singular subspaces of Tδ to those of T (via Wedin's sin-Θ theorem), and interpretable 'good'/'bad' scenario corollaries that quantify when one feature can replace k spurious ones.

Experiments are well-designed to test the theory: a synthetic setting with full control over alignment, a new and carefully justified harder dSprites structural function (h_new) with alignment verification in Appendix D.2 (Figure 5), and an OPE extension demonstrating broadened applicability of spectral NPIV.

The paper is honest about limitations: the unbounded optimality gap ε_d is acknowledged as an open problem, the δ-selection heuristics are presented with their weaknesses (Section 6.4, D.8), and rank-K perturbations are explicitly deferred to future work. The discussion in D.8 about the unprincipled nature of 2SLS-loss model selection is a valuable side contribution.
weaknesses: The headline theoretical guarantees are conditional in an important way. Theorem 4 controls the approximation error through the optimality gap ε_d(θ, ω, δ), but the paper explicitly notes this quantity is not bounded for neural network feature learning ('an open problem in its own right'). Thus the end-to-end generalization story for the practical algorithm remains incomplete, and the 'bad scenario' corollary is best read as a conditional result.

The 'bad scenario' analysis assumes knowledge that is unavailable in practice: the partition N={k} identifying which singular function h0 aligns with, and a favorable signal-to-noise condition. The practical prescription (choose δ large enough that γ_1(δ)>0) requires the very alignment information the method is meant to recover, leaving δ selection heuristic (two candidate procedures are proposed, both acknowledged as lacking theoretical justification — Section D.8).

Experimental evidence, while supportive, is somewhat narrow: comparisons are limited to DFIV and KIV on semi-synthetic dSprites data; the OPE results are mixed (AugSpecIV excels on Cartpole but underperforms on Mountain Car), and the authors themselves note no method performed uniformly well. Number of repetitions (9-16 fits) is modest. No real-data economic application is included despite the motivating example.

Assumption 3 (positive measure of ill-posedness of the learned feature spaces) is strong and feature-dependent; while Proposition 8 relates it to the approximation error, verifying it for learned features in practice is not discussed.

Some claims of improvement over prior work are overstated relative to the delta: Theorem 1 is described as improving on [8], but the improvement (high probability vs. in-expectation, sub-Gaussian tails) is incremental; the main novelty lies in the approximation error analysis, which, as noted, is conditional.

strengths: The core idea is elegant and well-motivated: outcome-awareness in spectral feature learning for NPIV is achieved by a rank-one augmentation of the conditional expectation operator T with the outcome regression r0, turning the modified contrastive loss into a best rank-d approximation of the augmented operator T_delta (Prop. 4.1). This gives a clean operator-theoretic bridge from the loss to downstream guarantees.

The theoretical analysis is substantive: a high-probability, representation-agnostic 2SLS excess-risk bound (Thm 5.1), a careful perturbation analysis (Wedin sin-Theta plus Weyl) that relates the singular subspaces of T_delta back to those of T (Thm C.6, Props C.1-C.5), and explicit 'good'/'bad' scenario corollaries showing that the outcome-aware method can recover a structural function aligned with a low singular function of T using d=1 features while standard SpecIV would need d>=k. The excess-loss-to-operator-gap bound (Prop A.4) is stated to be new even for delta=0, which is a genuine standalone contribution.

Experiments are thoughtfully designed and honest: a controlled synthetic setting where alignment and spectral decay are parameterized, a new, harder dSprites structural function (h_new, rotation-based) with empirical verification of the spectral misalignment diagnosis, and an OPE experiment where dynamic spectral misalignment naturally arises. The appendix includes an extensive naive outcome-aware baseline study, post-hoc rejection analysis, and rank-K perturbation preliminaries, which strengthen the credibility of the empirical claims.

Limitations are discussed candidly: the guarantees are explicitly conditioned on successful representation learning (small population optimality gap), the theoretical justification for second-stage-loss model selection is shown to be lacking (Sec E.8), and the authors clearly flag that driving Delta_delta to zero by DNN training is left open.

The comparison to the closely related Bruns-Smith (2025) work is fair and specific, distinguishing the method by requiring the Z-features to also be useful for the IV problem without post-hoc testing, and requiring weaker restrictions on ill-posedness for strong-norm convergence.
weaknesses: The main statistical guarantees are conditional: they control downstream 2SLS error given a small population optimality gap E_d of the learned features, but the paper provides no optimization or generalization theory for actually achieving small E_d with neural networks (acknowledged as open). The end-to-end story thus relies on empirical performance rather than a complete guarantee.

Delta selection remains partly heuristic. The three proposed procedures (estimated alignment, loss-balance heuristic, second-stage loss) are practical but lack consistency guarantees; notably, the theory-aware alignment estimator A(delta) becomes unstable precisely when delta grows large (||omega||->1), which is the regime where the 'bad scenario' guarantees apply. The chosen 5%-relative-improvement rule is ad hoc.
The code repository link appears to be blank in the manuscript ('can be found at .'), which is a reproducibility concern for the reproduction of figures.

Baseline coverage is somewhat narrow: DFIV, KIV and vanilla SpecIV are included, but there is no direct empirical comparison against the most closely related adaptive method (Bruns-Smith, 2025) beyond conceptual discussion; the appendix baseline is an in-house variant rather than that published method.

Some parts of the theory follow fairly directly from standard tools (Wedin sin-Theta, Weyl, Bernstein inequalities) combined with the Meunier et al. (2026) framework, so novelty is concentrated in the augmentation formulation and its consequences rather than new analytic machinery; the improvement over Theorem B.1 of Chen & Christensen (2018) (in-probability vs in-expectation) is real but incremental in scope.

Practical gains in well-aligned regimes (h_old dSprites, small c_alpha synthetic) are modest (~20% improvement) and depend on careful delta tuning, while large delta can clearly degrade performance; the method's robustness to miscalibrated delta is asserted empirically but not theoretically.

strengths: The core operator-theoretic contribution is clean and convincing: Proposition 4.1 establishes that the proposed contrastive loss is exactly a Hilbert–Schmidt best rank-d approximation of the augmented operator Tδ = [T | δr0], giving a principled interpretation of what the outcome-aware regularization is doing rather than an ad hoc heuristic.

The theoretical analysis is more careful than typical for this area: the paper separates a representation-agnostic high-probability 2SLS bound (Theorem 5.1, improving on the in-expectation guarantees of Chen & Christensen 2018) from a perturbation-based approximation analysis (Theorem C.6, Propositions C.3–C.5) that explicitly quantifies when the augmentation fixes spectral misalignment, including the informative 'good'/'bad' scenario comparisons against Meunier et al. (2026). The loss-to-operator-gap bound (Proposition A.4) is a useful standalone technical tool.

The paper is unusually honest about limitations: it states that end-to-end guarantees would require architecture-specific optimization/generalization analysis left open, admits that stage-2 loss selection for δ lacks theoretical justification, and analyzes the instability of the plug-in alignment estimator (∥ω∥→1) in Appendix E.9. This transparency supports reliable interpretation of the results.

The experimental design addresses the failure mode head-on: a new, harder dSprites benchmark (hnew) is constructed with a documented argument (Figure 5, E.1–E.2) for why it exhibits spectral misalignment, and appendix comparisons to naive outcome-aware baselines and rank-K extensions show the authors took alternative designs seriously rather than only comparing against weak strawmen.

Experiments span three regimes (controlled synthetic, image-based semi-synthetic, OPE in RL), and in the misaligned regimes the improvement over SpecIV is large and consistent with the theory's predictions.
weaknesses: The theoretical guarantees are conditional rather than end-to-end: all downstream bounds require a small population optimality gap Ed(θ̂m, ω̂m, δ), and the paper explicitly leaves open the question of whether empirical DNN training achieves this. Thus the theory does not actually establish that the practical estimator is consistent or robust; it characterizes the target the loss should reach.

The choice of δ—a new hyperparameter central to the method—rests on three heuristics, two of which the authors themselves show are problematic: the alignment-based estimator becomes ill-conditioned as δ grows (Appendix E.9), and stage-2 loss selection is admitted to be 'generally unprincipled.' In the OPE experiments δ is tuned as a generic hyperparameter via the very stage-2 loss whose validity is disputed. Practical deployment guidance is therefore weak.

Experimental support is narrower than the framing suggests: the headline misalignment results rely on a benchmark the authors constructed themselves; comparisons are largely limited to DFIV, KIV, and SpecIV, with no minimax/GMM baselines (e.g., AGMM-style methods) in the main NPIV experiments; and OPE results are mixed by the authors' own account (no method performed uniformly well, AugSpecIV and SpecIV 'struggled on Mountain Car'), which tempers the claimed breadth of applicability.

The methodological delta over SpecIV (Sun et al., 2025) is modest: a rank-one augmentation of the operator plus a quadratic penalty term. Much of the machinery (contrastive loss, 2SLS pipeline, spectral analysis framework) is inherited, so the contribution's novelty rests mainly on the perturbation analysis of the augmented operator. Appendix G further shows a simpler two-stage baseline is competitive when its fits are stable, which limits the practical significance of the added machinery.

Reproducibility is compromised: the appendix states the reproduction code 'can be found at .' with the URL missing/blank. Combined with substantial hyperparameter grids (Tables 4–5), an ad hoc 5%-relative-improvement acceptance rule for δ, and a post-hoc rejection rule for the naive baseline, exact replication of the reported figures would be difficult without the code.

Several conditions in the theory are uncheckable in practice (e.g., positivity of the spectral gap γd(δ) in Eq. (8), the signal-to-noise condition ∥s1∥ ≫ λk^{-2}∥q1∥, Eq. (15) requiring κ ≤ 1/2), so the 'bad scenario' guarantee is more of a qualitative explanation than a usable certificate that the method will succeed on a given problem.

strengths: The core idea is clean and well-motivated: the paper identifies a genuine, precisely characterized limitation of outcome-agnostic spectral feature learning (SpecIV), namely that the structural function may lie in low-singular-value regions of the conditional expectation operator, and proposes an elegant fix by augmenting the operator with an outcome-aligned column (T_delta = [T | delta r0]). The equivalence between the contrastive loss with the projection regularizer and the best rank-d approximation of the augmented operator (Proposition 4.1) is a satisfying operator-theoretic characterization that directly bridges the loss to downstream estimation error.

The theoretical analysis is substantial and complete. The paper provides (i) a general high-probability 2SLS excess-risk bound (Theorem 5.1) that improves on Chen & Christensen (2018) by holding with high probability under sub-Gaussian assumptions, (ii) a careful perturbation analysis (Wedin sin-Theta, Weyl's inequality) relating the singular subspaces of the augmented operator back to those of T, yielding guarantees for both 'good' and 'bad' alignment scenarios, and (iii) a new loss-to-operator-gap bound (Proposition A.4) that is claimed to be new even for the standard SpecIV setting. All proofs appear complete and correct as far as I can verify, including the technical details in Appendices A-D.

The empirical evaluation is unusually thorough for this area: controlled synthetic experiments where all parameters of T are tunable, a genuinely new and harder dSprites structural function (h_new) motivated by a careful spectral-alignment analysis (Section E.1-E.2, Figures 5-6), an OPE experiment demonstrating the method's applicability to the non-compact-operator setting via an iterative FQE-like procedure, and comparisons against DFIV, SpecIV, and KIV.

The paper is commendably honest about limitations and negative results: it explicitly acknowledges that downstream guarantees are conditional on small representation-learning optimality gap, that no DNN optimization/generalization analysis is provided (Section 5), that 2SLS-loss-based hyperparameter selection lacks theoretical justification and is 'generally unprincipled' (Section E.8), and it rigorously evaluates and discusses a naive outcome-aware baseline including its instability (Section G, Figures 17-19).

Practical considerations are addressed, including three distinct strategies for selecting delta with empirical support, numerical stabilization of the loss (Eq. 5), and a discussion of why the plug-in alignment estimator becomes unstable as delta grows (Section E.9), which formalizes an observed empirical phenomenon.
weaknesses: The main theoretical guarantees are conditional: the error bounds in the 'bad' scenario assume that the structural function is aligned with a known, specific singular function v_k and that the signal-to-noise ratio dominates lambda_k^{-2}, and the analysis presumes a favorable partition of the spectrum (N_bar) is chosen. In practice, the practitioner does not know where h_0 lies in the spectrum, so the theory does not fully close the loop between the motivating failure mode and the deployed method; the link is only via the empirical delta-selection heuristics, which are themselves partly ad hoc (Section 6.4).

The paper does not establish that the contrastive objective is actually optimized to small excess loss by the neural network training used in practice; the population-level optimality results (Proposition 4.1) and the empirical results are connected only heuristically. This is acknowledged but it means the central end-to-end claim (outcome-aware features fix spectral misalignment) rests substantially on the experiments rather than theory.

Empirical results are not uniformly favorable: in the OPE experiments, AugSpecIV and SpecIV show opposite task-dependent trends relative to DFIV (good on Cartpole, poor on Mountain Car), and the authors concede no OPE method performed uniformly well (Section 6.3). The dSprites improvement over DFIV in the h_new setting is 'match or slightly exceed,' so the practical advantage beyond the standard SpecIV baseline is demonstrated mainly on the authors' own new benchmark and the synthetic setting.

The method introduces a hyperparameter (delta) whose role in the guarantees is delicate: the theory requires delta large enough for a positive spectral gap but not so large that the regularizer dominates the loss (Section 6.4), and the proposed selection rules are heuristics without consistency guarantees (as the authors themselves note for the stage-2 loss approach).

Reproducibility statement is incomplete: the code link in Appendix E is blank ('can be found at .'), which undermines the otherwise good experimental documentation; the reviewer cannot verify code availability from the manuscript.

The contribution is an incremental but well-executed extension of SpecIV (Sun et al., 2025) and the analysis framework of Meunier et al. (2026); the novelty is real (outcome-awareness via operator augmentation, new loss-to-gap bound) but the overall conceptual step is modest, and the most general setting (rank-K perturbations) is deferred to future work with only preliminary, inconclusive results (Section F, Figure 16).
